items.prompt:
*The question below is followed by two statements numbered I and II. Decide whether the data given in the statements are sufficient to answer the question.*

Five persons — A, B, C, D and E — each has a different height.
**Who is the shortest among A, B, C, D and E?**

**I.** C is shorter than both A and D. B is taller than C but shorter than E.
**II.** A is taller than only one person. D is taller than A.
options: The data in statement I alone are sufficient to answer the question, while the data in statement II alone are not sufficient
The data in statement II alone are sufficient to answer the question, while the data in statement I alone are not sufficient
The data either in statement I alone or in statement II alone are sufficient to answer the question
The data in both the statements I and II together are necessary to answer the question
The data in both the statements I and II together are not sufficient to answer the question

steps: From I, C is shorter than A, D and B, and E is taller than B, so nobody is shorter than C.
Statement I alone: C is the shortest → **sufficient**.
Statement II alone: the shortest could be B, C or E (e.g. the order C > D > E > A > B gives B, while the order B > D > E > A > C gives C) → **not sufficient**.
Hence I alone is sufficient → option A.
solution.shortcut: Write the persons in a column from the top and place each clue; only the asked position needs to be fixed, not the whole order.
solution.trap: Statement II looks useful but still leaves more than one answer — do not upgrade to “both together” (D) or “either” (C) when only I works alone.

Five persons — J, K, L, M and N — each has a different weight.
**How many persons are heavier than M?**

**I.** M is heavier than J but lighter than L. K is the heaviest.
**II.** N is lighter than M. J is heavier than only one person.
options: The data in statement I alone are sufficient to answer the question, while the data in statement II alone are not sufficient
The data in statement II alone are sufficient to answer the question, while the data in statement I alone are not sufficient
The data either in statement I alone or in statement II alone are sufficient to answer the question
The data in both the statements I and II together are necessary to answer the question
The data in both the statements I and II together are not sufficient to answer the question

steps: I gives K > … > L > M > J, but N can sit anywhere below K. II puts J fourth (only one person is lighter than J).
Together: K is first and J fourth, so L and M take places 2 and 3 with L above M; N is fifth. Exactly two persons (K and L) are heavier than M.
Statement I alone: the number of persons heavier than M could be 2 or 3 (e.g. the order K > L > M > J > N gives 2, while the order K > L > N > M > J gives 3) → **not sufficient**.
Statement II alone: the number of persons heavier than M could be 0, 1 or 2 (e.g. the order M > K > L > J > N gives 0, while the order K > M > L > J > N gives 1) → **not sufficient**.
I and II together: exactly 2 persons are heavier than M → **sufficient**.
Hence both I and II together are needed → option D.
solution.shortcut: Write the persons in a column from the top and place each clue; only the asked position needs to be fixed, not the whole order.
solution.trap: Neither statement alone is enough, but do not stop at E — combine them and test again.

items.prompt:
*The question below is followed by two statements numbered I and II. Decide whether the data given in the statements are sufficient to answer the question.*

Arun, Bina and some other students stand in a row facing north.
**How many students are there in the row?**

**I.** Arun is 14th from the left end and Bina is 9th from the right end.
**II.** If Arun and Bina interchange their positions, Arun becomes 17th from the left end and Bina becomes 12th from the right end.
options: The data in statement I alone are sufficient to answer the question, while the data in statement II alone are not sufficient
The data in statement II alone are sufficient to answer the question, while the data in statement I alone are not sufficient
The data either in statement I alone or in statement II alone are sufficient to answer the question
The data in both the statements I and II together are necessary to answer the question
The data in both the statements I and II together are not sufficient to answer the question

steps: After the interchange Arun stands at Bina’s old place, so Bina is 17th from the left; Bina stands at Arun’s old place, so Arun is 12th from the right.
Together: Bina is 17th from the left (II) and 9th from the right (I), so the row has 17 + 9 − 1 = 25 students (check: Arun 14th from left is 25 − 14 + 1 = 12th from right).

Statement I alone: the number of students could be 14, 15, 16 and more (e.g. Arun 14th and Bina 6th from the left in a row of 14 gives 14 students, while Arun 14th and Bina 7th from the left in a row of 15 gives 15 students) → **not sufficient**.

Statement II alone: the number of students could be 17, 18, 19 and more (e.g. Arun 6th and Bina 17th from the left in a row of 17 gives 17 students, while Arun 7th and Bina 17th from the left in a row of 18 gives 18 students) → **not sufficient**.
I and II together: there are 25 students → **sufficient**.
Hence both I and II together are needed → option D.
solution.shortcut: Total = (position from one end) + (position from the other end) − 1. A position counted from one end needs the total before it can be turned into a position from the other end.
solution.trap: Statement II looks complete because it gives two positions, but they belong to two different persons; one person’s place from both ends is needed.

steps: I: if k persons are taller than F, then k persons are shorter than E and F is above E, so (F, E) is 1st & 7th, 2nd & 6th or 3rd & 5th.
II: G is first and three persons come between G and E, so E is fifth. With I, F is third.
Statement I alone: the third tallest could be A, B, C, D, F or G (e.g. the order B > F > A > C > D > E > G gives A, while the order A > F > B > C > D > E > G gives B) → **not sufficient**.

I and II together: F is the third tallest → **sufficient**.
Hence both I and II together are needed → option D.

solution.trap: Neither statement alone is enough, but do not stop at E — combine them and test again.

steps: I: if x persons scored fewer marks than N, then x + 1 scored more than M, and M is above N; so (M, N) is 2nd & 7th, 3rd & 6th or 4th & 5th.
II: P is two places from M, with J and K below P. Together, P can be 1st (M 3rd, N 6th) or 2nd (M 4th, N 5th) — P’s place is not fixed.

Statement I alone: the number of persons scoring more marks than P could be 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 or 6 (e.g. the order P > J > K > M > N > L > Q gives 0, while the order J > P > K > M > N > L > Q gives 1) → **not sufficient**.

Statement II alone: the number of persons scoring more marks than P could be 0, 1, 2, 3 or 4 (e.g. the order P > J > M > K > L > N > Q gives 0, while the order L > P > J > M > K > N > Q gives 1) → **not sufficient**.

I and II together: the number of persons scoring more marks than P could be 0, 1 or 3 (e.g. the order P > J > M > K > L > N > Q gives 0, while the order L > P > J > M > N > K > Q gives 1) → **not sufficient**.
Hence even I and II together are not sufficient → option E.

solution.trap: Combining the statements narrows the possibilities, but more than one answer still survives — a guess from one convenient case is not sufficiency.
